REQUIRED_FIELDS.why: Report 1 leaves the Washington and Colorado penalty cells as unpriced labels and never mentions the applicability thresholds that decide whether a pre-launch app is in scope at all, whereas Report 2 carries every penalty with its unit, the Colorado breach-response duty, and a consent spec he could hand straight to engineering.

LAUNCH_DECISION.why: Both give a short, bounded danger list up top, but Report 2's test is visibly applied to this product — who can sue, what the ceiling is, and which duties actually reach a company with no users yet — while Report 1's list rests on private right of action plus AG aggressiveness alone.

DENSITY.why: Report 1 is tighter word-for-word, but several of its rows read like answers without carrying a number, whereas Report 2 answers all five questions in one table, packs four states × ten fields into one screen, and ends with an owner-tagged action list — even after deleting its off-question auto-renewal and minors detours.

GROUNDING.why: Both avoid the one error that would have mattered — neither treats Illinois damages as per-scan and both name the 2024 fix — so this turns on verified cells, and Report 2 lands more of them (the $7,500 and $20,000 figures, Colorado's district-attorney enforcement and breach-response protocol, Texas having no written-policy mandate, e-signature confirmed, retroactivity) plus explicit open questions for counsel, against Report 1's unpriced cells and a BNSF judgment presented without its later history.

OVERALL.why: Report 2 is the one you can look a state up in and actually build from — every dedicated statute's five cells filled with units, the wider sensitive-data layer differentiated rather than lumped, thresholds that tell you what applies to you today, and a retention rule tied to your once-at-signup scan instead of Report 1's default of holding templates for up to a year or three.
